news.title: Jan. 6 should follow Trump 'to his grave,' Biden says in new memoir
news.text:
Former President Joseph Biden claims his successor was desperate to hang on to power after losing the 2020 election, saying, "What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave."

Biden has harsh words for Donald Trump in his new memoir, "Promise Me, America," which goes on sale Nov. 17. He denounces Trump's decision to grant sweeping pardons and clemency to Jan. 6 defendants on his first day back in office and admonishes Trump for not holding a formal ceremony honoring the officers who defended the Capitol.

Early excerpts of the memoir were published Monday by The Atlantic.

Biden also reveals what happened inside the Oval Office during his nearly two-hour meeting with then President-elect Trump in November of 2024, describing a friendly tone from Trump that "bordered on fawning."

Trump defeated Kamala Harris to win the presidency after Biden withdrew from the race in July of 2024.

Oval Office meeting

Biden said he was taken aback by how warmly Trump greeted him just eight days after the bruising 2024 election. 

"Trump was immediately chatty and surprised me by adopting a tone so friendly that I thought he might be putting me on," Biden writes, adding that Trump told him, "You know, Joe, if it weren’t for politics, I believe we’d be good friends."

Biden said he was "too stunned to respond" and that Trump continued "as if intoxicated by the curious conversational path he had chosen."

"Yes, if it weren’t for politics, we’d spend all our time golfing together," Trump said, according to Biden.

Trump called Biden’s record on job creation "extraordinary" and, according to Biden, "relieved he didn’t have to run against me."

Biden said he cut off the compliments to move on to the business at hand, but as he gave a wide-ranging overview of issues that could define the Trump presidency, he noticed Trump was more focused on personalities of world leaders.

"As if we were sharing gossip about people at a dinner party, not discussing issues of global significance," Biden wrote.

Indictment of Trump’s second term

Biden said Trump’s "lies" have "kept coming" since taking office -- starting with the "utterly discredited claim that he had defeated me in 2020.”

"And they gained momentum as Trump took a wrecking ball to our traditions and institutions—at times literally, as when he tore down the East Wing of the White House (after promising that he would not)," Biden writes. The Electoral College certified Biden's victory in December of 2020.

Biden acknowledged that the policies of presidents are vulnerable to politics and can be undone at the whims of their successor, but argued "that feeling was magnified by the dismissive and destructive nature of Donald Trump.”

He said Trump "seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down."

Biden took issue with Trump’s decision to again withdraw from the Paris climate accords, open public lands to drilling for oil, end support for electric vehicles and cancel wind and solar projects, making it harder for the U.S. to compete with China.

"Trump announced these policies at a rally as, at a five-star hotel across from the White House, oil and gas executives sipped champagne and nibbled on Pop-Tarts emblazoned with his image," he said.

He criticized DOGE as well as Trump’s decision to cut federal funding to Democratic states with no explanation, gut nonprofits and withdraw from the World Health Organization.

"It was clearly going to be a crueler government," Biden said.

"It was also going to be a government that stoked racial tensions instead of calming them," he added. "The new administration would launch a campaign to end the birthright-citizenship protections of the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution, a proud legacy of the Civil War. ICE officers would comb American cities, using expanded police powers to round up brown and Black people and detain them far from the courts and local police. We would be a less tolerant society, with raging conspiracy theories actively promoted by the White House and Trump’s constant and increasingly unhinged social-media feed."

Presidential immunity and the Supreme Court

Biden opened up about the 2024 Supreme Court decision that ruled presidents have some immunity from prosecution for acts that fall within their official duties.

"There was no precedent for that ruling," he said. "Common sense didn’t support it. There was no constitutional basis for it. It was inexplicable. Indefensible. And a death knell for accountability."

The former president warned that "no nation can survive character-free leadership for long" and that the U.S. is "no exception to that rule."
news.summary: Biden also said Trump "bordered on fawning" during 2024 Oval Office meeting
news.author: Justin Gomez

news.title: Biden Reveals Weird Trump Moment That Left Him Speechless
news.text:
Joe Biden was left momentarily speechless when Donald Trump bizarrely suggested they could have been golfing buddies in another life, the former president has revealed.

Just eight days after defeating Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, Trump used an Oval Office meeting with his longtime political rival to say they would have made good friends if it weren’t for politics, Biden revealed in an excerpt from his new memoir, Promise Me, America.

The 83-year-old also claims Trump showered him with compliments about his presidency and admitted he was relieved he never had to face him at the ballot box.

In an account published by The Atlantic, Biden revealed the bizarre exchange happened as he hosted Trump at the White House for the traditional presidential transition meeting. Trump did not offer Biden the same courtesy after his defeat in the 2020 election.

According to Biden, Trump adopted a surprisingly warm tone that caught him off guard.

“He was immediately chatty and surprised me by adopting a tone so friendly that I thought he might be putting me on,” Biden wrote. “It bordered on fawning.”

Biden then recalled Trump making an unexpected personal remark.

“You know, Joe, if it weren’t for politics, I believe we’d be good friends,” Trump reportedly told him.

The president-elect continued, suggesting that the two could have hit the links together.

“Yes, if it weren’t for politics, we’d spend all our time golfing together,” Trump said, according to Biden’s account.

But the compliments did not stop there.

Biden wrote that Trump praised his administration’s job-creation record, describing his performance as “extraordinary.” Trump also admitted that he had been relieved that he did not have to run against Biden in the 2024 presidential election.

Biden said he was so surprised by the conversation that he struggled to respond.

“I think I blinked, too stunned to respond,” he recalled.

The former president admitted he did not understand why Trump was being so complimentary and decided to interrupt the exchange to focus on the purpose of their meeting.

“I didn’t really understand why he was buttering me up, so I cut off his compliments to move on to the business at hand,” Biden wrote.

The meeting was initially scheduled to last 30 minutes but eventually stretched to nearly two hours.

Biden said he used the opportunity to brief Trump on major international issues, including Ukraine, Russia, NATO, Gaza and the Middle East, China, and relations across the Americas and Africa.

However, Biden said Trump seemed more interested in the personalities of world leaders than in the broader geopolitical issues being discussed.

Biden and Trump have had a deeply antagonistic relationship over the years.

Trump began targeting Biden personally in 2018, calling him “Crazy Joe” and describing him as “weak, both mentally and physically” after Biden suggested he would have confronted Trump over his treatment of women. Trump also warned that Biden would go down “fast and hard” in a physical fight. 

When Biden announced his 2020 presidential campaign, Trump quickly branded him “Sleepy Joe,” questioning his energy, intelligence, and mental sharpness. He also called him “low IQ” and mocked his verbal stumbles during campaign rallies. Trump later added “Crooked Joe” to his collection of nicknames, accusing Biden of corruption without establishing those allegations as fact. 

The insults continued throughout Biden’s presidency, with Trump repeatedly portraying him as confused, incompetent, and incapable of carrying out his duties. He also mocked Biden’s public appearances and sometimes imitated his movements and speech. 

Meanwhile, Biden has repeatedly portrayed Trump as a threat to democracy.

But Trump’s obsession with Biden didn’t stop after he left the White House in January 2025.

Biden, who has largely retired from public life after being diagnosed with stage four cancer, has become Trump’s go-to target for problems ranging from inflation and immigration to military shortages and foreign policy.

news.title: Donald Trump Defends Iran War as He Takes Aim at JD Vance's Remarks on Conflict: 'A Lot of People Didn't Like His Comments'
news.text:
Donald Trump has defended his decision to go to war with Iran after Vice President J.D. Vance blamed the conflict on the midterm elections disaster, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

 The president, 80, increased rumors of tension between himself and the veep by pushing back on comments Vance made on social media regarding the war.Trump Questions Vance Social Media CommentsTrump stated Vance, 42, should have commented on whether he would make the same decision again while giving his opinion on the controversial move.

Speaking to reporters in Washington on Sunday night, Trump said: "He was right, other than one thing." 

"He should have made one other statement," the president added — posing the question to himself: "'If you had it to do again, would you do it again?' The answer is yes."

The Commander-in-Chief insisted Vance's comments had not affected their relationship, but did suggest they had not been well received by all.

He said: "A lot of people didn't like his comments. But not me."President Stands By His Decision — Despite Vance's CommentsIn an interview on CBS’ 60 Minutes that aired Sunday night, Trump said he didn't know whether Vance would make the same call again. His own answer, he said, was "an emphatic yes, because you can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon."

The president’s comments come after Vance, on Wednesday, wrote "the reason we lost is the war," in a lengthy post after Democrats won both chambers of Congress. 

He challenged Republicans who backed the war to say whether it was worth losing the Senate and argued that many voters who backed Trump in 2024 had switched to Democrats.'Everyone Knows Why We Lost'The veep wrote: "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

"But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

While many political pundits were shocked to see Vance call out the president, Trump's son, Don Jr., approved as well, retweeting the entire message and enthusiastically commenting, "Every word of this is..." 

Vance wasn't the only one among Trump's supposed allies to express surprise at the election results. 

Former Trump chief strategist Steve Bannon, one of the president's most loyal supporters, confessed that Republicans had a historically bad showing Tuesday night, especially among male voters.Men typically make up one of the strongest MAGA demographics, but Tuesday's elections revealed that loyalty seems to be evaporating. 

According to NBC News exit polling, male voters were split almost evenly between Republican and Democratic candidates. That's a significant swing from the 2024 presidential elections, which saw Trump win the male vote by a whopping 12 percentage points.

In that race, Trump won 55 percent of male voters, compared with Kamala Harris's 43 percent. The reversal seemed to stun Bannon.

"That can’t be right," he said during the election-night broadcast on Real America's Voice. "That’s a massive problem. That will roll through and have consequences."

news.title: DeSantis: Time for a 'Bottom-Up' Reform of Conservative Media
news.text:
Fact check: Probably true. And largely moot, or at least it will be soon enough.

Ron DeSantis made an appearance Saturday at the University of Notre Dame, ostensibly to analyze the midterm debacle for the GOP, but also clearly to establish himself as a post-midterm leader among Republicans. The outgoing governor of Florida spoke about the necessary changes to the conservative movement to return to success, and focused on the conservative media, at least briefly. Michael Tracey refers to this as DeSantis' "I Told You So" tour, which references a similar criticism DeSantis made at the beginning of the 2024 primaries after DeSantis dropped out:

Ron DeSantis, continuing his post-midterms "I Told You So" tour, says there needs to be a "big change" in "conservative media culture" -- because so much that is just a "grift," and/or "pay-to-play" scam-artistry stuff. Please note: This is obviously an implicit critique of "MAGA Media Inc.," and therefore "Trump," since to the degree there's been any GOP media "grifting" in recent years -- which according to DeSantis has contaminated the right-wing information landscape -- it's all been overwhelmingly centered around the personage of one man: Our Favorite President. DeSantis actually briefly started to complain about this phenomenon at the tail-end of the 2024 Republican primaries, right before he got knocked out in Iowa.— Michael Tracey (@mtracey) November 7, 2026

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) called for a “big change” in conservative media after the Democrats trounced the Republicans in the midterms, with the gov saying a whole lot of “grift” needs to be purged in order for the GOP to win over voters in the years ahead. DeSantis shared his take during a Saturday interview at the University of Notre Dame.“I think you need more bottom-up, I think you need less focus on the presidency, and I think you need more focus on not just people running for elected office, people that are involved in the conservative groups, [but] I think we need a big change in kind of the conservative media culture,” DeSantis said. “Because a lot of that is a grift, and it’s pay-to-play, and it’s just not offering very much in the way of strong ideas and things that are really going to illuminate your understanding.”He continued, “There’s all these different things that are not doing well on the right, and I think we deserve an American Right that’s fit to fight and is ready to go for… a decade of battles, just to get to a point where we’re able to avert disaster and put us on a solid path.”

Well, as far as the "I told you so" aspect, that doesn't really work. Trump won the primaries and then went on to a resounding win in the 2024 general election. That doesn't necessarily make those criticisms invalid, but those issues didn't prevent Trump from winning and the GOP from maintaining their thin congressional majorities either. 

In this cycle, DeSantis may have a point, given the sharp disconnect between the cheerleading from the supposed "grifters" and last week's debacle. But again, how salient is it really? Yes, there are Trump cheerleaders and sycophants in the media but in the era of social media, it's pretty easy to find MAGAs and Never Trumpers and all points in between among conservative media. Most commentators focus on policies and outcomes, and in our binary system, that generally means that conservatives line up behind Donald Trump – not because of Trump himself, but to get as many of their preferred policies put and kept in place. In this midterm, the choice seemed pretty stark between the two parties, given that one party wrapped itself completely around Trump and his rallies while the other welcomed socialists and Islamists into their "big tent." That's not a mirage; that was the reality of this cycle and perhaps the next six years in the Senate. 

Besides, there is a difference between grifting and cheerleading. The latter is sincere, while the former is not. Most of the issue DeSantis identifies likely takes the latter form from people who sincerely believe in Trump's genius, not people who cynically pretend to do so just to get a few clicks. To put it mildly, the profit motive in the American media market cuts sharply in the other direction. Republican apostates and Right-leaning Trump critics get lots more attention and exposure on most media platforms. The "grift" potential narrows sharply for Trump acolytes. To the extent that the issue exists, it comes from true believers rather than "grifters."

Regardless, the issue will largely resolve itself on its own, especially after the midterm "shellacking." Trump can't run for another term anyway, and the reaction to his "vote like I'm on the ballot" tour makes it clear that the magic has dissipated. Trump will remain influential, but he's not the future of the Republican Party any longer. Republican voters will decide that future over the next two years, and the "cheerleader" faction will fracture and realign to other poles within the new firmament. 

That will be a true "bottom-up reform" of the conservative media. Perhaps its next iteration will have less of a hero-worship quality, mainly because there are no potential idols on the GOP's horizon, no sui generis figures to rally the less-engaged electorate. Democrats didn't have anyone after Barack Obama, although the Protection Racket Media tried mightily to lift both Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris to that status. The future of the GOP will likely belong to a well-seasoned politician with a substantial track record of success in elections and policymaking, not a celebrity tycoon with a gift for connecting with the working class and charming media influencers into cheerleading roles. 

DeSantis is right, but voters and readers have already begun the process. The end of the era approaches. The 'reform' will take care of itself. The larger issue is the mainstream media's corruption, and DeSantis also called that out in the same interview. That should be our focus in the short run until the 2028 sweepstakes get fully underway.

news.title: Numbers Don’t Lie: Where Black Voters Stand and What It Means for America After the Midterms
news.text:
The numbers are in, and America’s political landscape looks different after the 2026 midterms. A new New York Times analysis breaks down how voters across age, race and gender cast their ballots, revealing a shift toward Democrats after the gains Republicans made in 2024. For Black America, the findings raise bigger questions about political loyalty, the influence of younger voters and what these results say about the community’s expectations of political leadership.

Across nearly every major demographic, voters shifted toward Democrats, reversing much of the Republican momentum from 2024, according to The Times and an analysis from Tufts CIRCLE, a nonpartisan research center at Tufts University focused on youth civic engagement. Younger voters made some of the biggest moves, with voters under 30 swinging more than 30 percentage points toward Democrats.

The gender breakdown reveals another notable political shift: Men and women moved toward Democrats in 2026, with younger men showing one of the sharpest changes from their 2024 voting patterns.

Experts predicted the shift, citing President Donald Trump’s low approval rating and American concerns about the war in Iran, the cost of living and attacks on voting rights.

RELATED: The Funniest Memes Coming Out of the 2026 Midterms

“Part of the reason Trump’s approval ratings are so low is he’s pushing policies and pushing positions that are very unpopular, and so the conflict in Iran is a great example; the public understands that this was Trump’s decision, and they understand this connects to extremely high gas prices,” Peter Enns, a professor in the department of government at Cornell University, told TIME Magazine in October. 

With that, Gen Z made its presence felt in the 2026 midterms. According to the NYT analysis, voters under 30 shifted more than 30 percentage points toward Democrats compared with 2024. Young men moved nearly 40 points, challenging assumptions about their political direction. The results show a generation whose political loyalties are still evolving.

John Della Volpe, a left-leaning pollster, told NPR that younger people demanded that every party and candidate earn their vote this time around, which ended up working for the Democrats in the midterms. 

“The cohort of younger people in this cycle had a different set of experiences than the cohort of people two years ago, or four years before that,” he said. “Every candidate, every party has to earn their votes.” But the Black vote deserves its own conversation…

In 2024, Trump made notable inroads with Black voters, particularly Black men, whose support shifted 17 percentage points in his direction, PEW Research previously reported. Still, former Vice President Kamala Harris received approximately 86% of the Black vote. In 2026, Democratic support rebounded to levels closer to those seen in 2020. Among young Black men, the shift toward Democrats was approximately 25 percentage points, nearly reversing the movement toward Trump two years earlier.

The numbers suggest that the political conversation around Black men is more complicated than headlines about a mass departure from the Democratic Party might suggest. Black voters are not a monolith, and their political choices continue to reflect changing priorities, economic concerns and expectations of leadership.

Turnout adds another layer. According to the Brennan Center for Justice, preliminary Georgia voter data showed Black turnout increasing significantly compared with 2022, while white turnout declined. The racial turnout gap reached its lowest point in two decades. Among Georgians who voted in 2024, 24% of Black voters did not return to the polls in 2026, compared with more than 29% of white voters.

For Black Americans, the takeaway goes beyond party affiliation. These results highlight the importance of political participation, generational engagement and holding elected officials accountable. In the future, Americans are challenging politicians seeking support to demonstrate that they understand the communities behind the numbers.
news.summary:
From Black men to Gen Z, the midterms revealed a political reset. But the biggest takeaway may be what Black voters are saying about the direction of the country.

news.title: Fox News’ Declining Ratings, Explained — Is It Really Just ‘Viewer Fatigue’?
news.text:
Fox News contends the business is in “incredibly good shape.” Its viewership figures may suggest a different situation.

This October, Fox News’ audience levels were down 28 percent from October 2025, according to Nielsen statistics cited by the Los Angeles Times. Meanwhile, the total day audience among 25-to-54-year-old viewers dropped to 98,000, the cable news channel’s lowest monthly level for that metric in a quarter-century.

“The business is in incredibly good shape, and we’re very proud of the team,” Fox Corporation CEO and executive chairman Lachlan Murdoch told analysts in a recent quarterly earnings call, per the Times. “What we are seeing, though, is some viewer fatigue where our viewers have gone through some incredible news cycles the last few years.”

Murdoch argued that Fox News’ October 2026 viewership couldn’t compare to that of October 2025, when news stories like Donald Trump’s second presidential inauguration, Charlie Kirk’s assassination, DOGE’s government overhauls, and flooding disasters were still driving viewers to the channel. And the exec claimed that viewers weren’t leaving Fox News for rivals like MS NOW and CNN.

“Those viewers are not switching to another news channel; they are just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall,” he said, per The Hollywood Reporter. “We have seen this playbook, and we know how to move through it.”

But as the Times noted, MS NOW and CNN actually gained viewers in October. And indeed, MS NOW’s leadership, like Mark Lazarus, CEO of parent company Versant, isn’t sympathizing with Fox News’ fatigue issue. “We’re not… currently seeing any fatigue with our audiences,” Lazarus told analysts in his own quarterly call in early November, THR reports. “Our audiences are active and vibrant and growing … I think it’s a testament to the quality of our product, to the voices that we have on there, and to the trust that our viewers have in our brands and in our talent.”

FOX via Getty Images

The news gets worse for Fox News: October marked Fox’s lowest-rated month since December 2023, and the year-over-year decline suggested that “conservatives [were] tuning out ahead of the high-stakes elections,” Oliver Darcy wrote for the Status newsletter in October, per CNN. According to Variety, observers suspect conservatives were tuning out of Fox News faster than they were tuning out of CNN or MS NOW.

Murdoch and his colleagues at Fox News still have some bragging rights: Fox News still attracted more viewers in October than MS NOW and CNN combined, THR notes. But that ratings win doesn’t negate that Fox News’ October 2025-to-October 2026 decline was the largest pre-election dip the network has seen in the last six election cycles, according to THR.

It’s possible the ratings shift for the conservative Fox News reflects the political shift in the country, which experienced a “blue tsunami” with major Democratic wins during this month’s latest midterm elections. As the Times points out, such a correlation wouldn’t be unprecedented. During its MSNBC era, the liberal-leaning MS NOW lost viewers after Trump defeated Democratic presidential opponent Kamala Harris in 2024.

Michael Loccisano/Getty Images

Another issue for both Fox News and its rivals, the Times adds, is that the pay TV sector is suffering as customers drop their cable and satellite subscriptions for streaming — though, again, that trend doesn’t explain why Fox News lost viewers in October while MS NOW and CNN made gains.

If Lachlan had to face the music on Fox Corporation’s quarterly call with analysts, he might be relieved he didn’t have to do so after the midterm elections. On that Tuesday, Fox News averaged 4.3 million total viewers between 8 and 11 p.m., ranking behind broadcast TV channels NBC (6.7 million) and ABC (5.2 million), according to Nielsen figures cited by The Guardian. Fox News did defeat CNN (4.1 million) and MS NOW (3.7 million) that night, but CNN bested Fox News in the advertiser-coveted 25-to-54 demographic.

Laura Ingraham Facebook; Fox News

Viewer fatigue might also apply to Trump news, too. In his Reliable Sources newsletter, CNN’s Brian Stelter observed that Fox News was treading carefully in its coverage of Trump’s rallies. “This is coming from the top down,” a current Fox host told Stelter, adding that general thinking at the network was that “Trump doesn’t rate anymore.”

The Biggest Controversies in Fox News History

In an MS NOW opinion, media columnist Brian Lowry wrote that “as Trump’s act appears to have grown tired, even in the eyes of millions who voted for him, [Fox News] may be entering a perilous new phase.”

Trump, for his part, has his own explanation for Fox News’ recent decline. “Fox News Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!” he wrote in a Truth Social post this month. “All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it.”

Then Trump, whose approval rating is at an all-time low of -27, according to The Economist, offered his own spin on faltering performance metrics: “It’s them, not me — my numbers are better than they have ever been.”

Abdul El Sayed’s Win Is American Muslims’ Obama Moment. But a Backlash LoomsThere has also been some reluctance on the part of the Modi government to engage with the Democrats since President Trump came back to power in 2025. PM Modi hasn't had any one-to-one meetings with Democratic Party leaders in this period. Foreign Minister S Jaishankar's engagement with Democratic Party leaders have also been as part of bipartisan delegations.This reluctance may partly have been due to President Trump's increasingly hostile policy against India through his tariffs and public statements. There was speculation that Trump's hostility was due to PM Modi not meeting him during his US visit in 2024 on the eve of the Presidential election. This was a sensible decision from PM Modi's side in line with India's position not to get involved in the partisan rivalries in the US. Even within the larger debacle of the Republican Party, the Modi government has faced a few setbacks. Vivek Ramaswamy, who had openly expressed his admiration for PM Modi in the past, faced a defeat in the Ohio Governor election. Ramaswamy faced a great deal of flak during the campaign for backing an ad featuring the mother of his opponent, Amy Acton. The ad showed Acton's mother calling her a liar. The ad was used despite it being publicly known that Acton was abused by her stepfather as a teenager and her mother chose to back her abuser. Ramaswamy's fortunes were on the rise within the Republican Party as he was considered one of the brains behind Department of Governmental Efficiency (DOGE).Then another prominent backer of the Modi government, Tulsi Gabbard, resigned as Director of National Intelligence in the Trump government citing 'personal reasons'. She had differed with Trump on the war in Iran. The other problem within the Republican Party is the increasing anti-Indian sentiment in its base. Trump's moves against H1B visa was also seen as attempts to appease his base. This has also led to an overwhelming consolidation of Indian Americans behind the Democrats. In the mid-terms this was over 60 percent. The increasing racism from the right wing has undone whatever gains the Republicans had made among Indian Americans. American politics is in uncharted waters. In the next two years, the Modi government will have to balance between a wounded Trump and a resurgent Democratic Party with its competing factions. news.title: Trump told Biden they’d be ‘good friends’ if not for politics, ex-president reveals
news.text:
Former president Joe Biden has revealed that Donald Trump told him that if it weren’t for politics, he believed the pair would be “good friends.”

Writing in his upcoming memoir Promise Me, America, Biden shared how he was “surprised” at Trump’s “friendly” tone when the Democrat hosted the then-president-elect and his entourage at the White House in November 2024 – and claimed that Trump even complimented his time in office.

The former president claimed that Trump told him his performance on job creation had been “extraordinary” — and that he was relieved he didn’t have to run against him after he dropped out of the presidential race. It marked a significant shift in tone for Trump, who hurled insults, such as “Sleepy Joe,” at his predecessor on the campaign trail.

“Trump was immediately chatty and surprised me by adopting a tone so friendly that I thought he might be putting me on,” Biden wrote in an excerpt from his book published in The Atlantic. “It bordered on fawning.”

Biden, 83, recalled that Trump, 80, turned to him and said, “You know, Joe, if it weren’t for politics, I believe we’d be good friends.” 

“I think I blinked, too stunned to respond. Then he kept going, as if intoxicated by the curious conversational path he had chosen,” Biden recalled. 

Trump then apparently said to Biden, “Yes, if it weren’t for politics, we’d spend all our time golfing together.” The meeting in the Diplomatic Reception Room was scheduled for 30 minutes but ran nearly two hours, according to Biden. 

Biden was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer last year and said that his health meant he has had to scale back in-person events to promote his memoir. 

“Some days are better than others. It hasn't stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down,” Biden said in a social media post Sunday. “What that means is, unfortunately, I won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped. However, I’m hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves.”

Concern over Biden’s health and mental fitness dominated the end of his second term and 2024 presidential campaign. After intense scrutiny following a disastrous debate performance against Trump, former Vice President Kamala Harris stepped in for Biden and mounted an unsuccessful bid for the White House.

Critics accused the Biden administration of concealing the extent of the president’s health struggles and paving the way for the Democrats’ bruising 2024 loss.

Former first lady Jill Biden opened up about the impact of her husband’s cancer diagnosis while promoting her own book earlier this year. While she had previously expressed anger over the Democratic Party's treatment of Biden after the debate, she said she has reconciled with those feelings after the diagnosis.

“I think Joe’s cancer diagnosis, it really puts life into perspective and you really do appreciate each and every day and a lot of anger that you have, you think, ‘What’s the point?’ You know, ‘What is the point?’” she said on The View in June. “And I think that’s why Joe and I try to, you know, just take each day that comes and try to find the joys.”
news.summary: Biden shared how he was ‘surprised’ at Trump’s ‘friendly’ tone when he hosted the then-president-elect at the White House in November 2024

Joe Biden has hit back at claims in CNN host Jake Tapper’s book that the former president forgot his son had died of cancer. 

Excerpts of the paperback edition of Original Sin, obtained by Politico’s Playbook, contain new allegations of memory lapses during Biden’s term in office. 

At one point, according to the excerpt, “Biden seemed to think his son Beau, who died in 2015, was still alive and fighting cancer.”

A spokesperson for Biden denied the claim in a statement to Playbook: “There has not been a single day since May 30, 2015 when President Biden has not felt the pain of losing his son Beau to cancer, and for anyone to suggest otherwise, much less profit off that lie, speaks volumes about the character and credibility of the authors.”

Biden’s oldest son, Beau, a military veteran and twice-elected Delaware attorney general, died of brain cancer in 2015 at age 46. 

The new excerpts also suggest that Joe Biden appeared to have forgotten that Senator Bob Dole had died, despite having delivered a lengthy eulogy for him three years previously. 

Tapper and co-author Alex Thompson, an Axios political correspondent, have faced waves of criticism for releasing the book in May 2025, the same month as Biden’s cancer diagnosis announcement, as well as allegations that they haven’t placed allegations of Trump’s cognitive decline under the same scrutiny. 

Thompson defended the release of the edition in a post on X. 

“Read the book, make up your own mind. Paperback out Tuesday w/ new reporting,” he posted. 

The new edition’s release coincides with that of Biden’s own memoir, Promise Me, America.

In a podcast appearance last year, Tapper defended himself against claims he has ignored Trump’s health problems. 

“I understand that there are a lot of people out there who think I would take President Biden in a coma over Donald Trump. I understand,” said Tapper. 

“I don’t know anybody who thinks that he could be president right now and all the way through 2029 in his current state,” Tapper added of Biden.

The book claims that Biden’s aides shielded him from public scrutiny as his health deteriorated during his term in office. 

According to the book, Biden once forgot the name of actor George Clooney, as well as those of key officials. 

Biden’s disastrous performance in the 2024 presidential debate led him to step aside as a Democratic presidential candidate to make way for Kamala Harris, whom Trump defeated.

news.title: 'Election Nostradamus' reveals 'slam dunk number one pick' for 2028 presidential race
news.text:
A man dubbed the 'election Nostradamus' has revealed his 'slam dunk pick' for the 2028 Democratic Party presidential candidate.

Nate Silver predicted the Democrats would take control of the House of Representatives and the Senate at last week's midterms, and he's now detailed who he believes will take on the Republican Party in 2028.

While Kamala Harris and the outgoing Governor of California, Gavin Newsom, are largely regarded as the front runners to run for the White House, Silver believes the Democrats will get behind a different candidate.

Silver explained at the Crooked Con political conference on Saturday (November 7) that he believes Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff would be his 'slam dunk number one pick'.

"He won by what was like 16, 17, 18 points or something," the 'election Nostradamus' said, as per The Daily Beast.

"He seems like the uniformly ‘compromise candidate’ between the progressive and the more centrist factions of the party. And he seems very talented."

Silver suggested what he called was Ossoff's 'looksmaxxing' efforts could also play in his favor.

Ossoff made history in 2021 as he became Georgia’s first Jewish senator. He has spoken publicly at his disapproval of the Trump administration, previously dubbing the president as a 'national disgrace'.

The Democrat politician was up for re-election in the midterms last week, ultimately defeating Republican challenger Mike Collins by 59 percent to 41 percent.

In his victory speech, Ossoff claimed the midterm results were proof 'the American people have rejected the failed lame duck president Donald J. Trump'.

It remains a mystery as to who the Republican presidential candidate in 2028 could be, though one person who won't be running is Trump.

Under the 22nd Amendment of the United States Constitution, no person can be elected to the office of the president more than twice, meaning the president is unable to run in two years time.

That hasn't stopped Trump from floating the idea that he could run for POTUS again, saying during a rally in Iowa last month that he possesses the 'right to run'.

He did concede though that the 'law says that I'm not allowed to'.

Meanwhile, the POTUS said earlier this year he “would love to run” for a third term, but ultimately conceded that 'the law is very strong' when it comes to prohibiting it.

“The law is very strong on that,” Trump said. “The 22nd Amendment is very clear, and I believe in following the law.”

news.title: Trump should carry Jan. 6 riots ‘to his grave,’ Biden says in memoir
news.text:
Former U.S. President Joe Biden writes in his White House memoir that Donald Trump, at once his predecessor and successor, has deeply damaged the country and world with an administration determined to “tear down institutions and inflame hatreds.”

And the 83-year-old Democrat said the 80-year-old Trump’s years of lies about his 2020 defeat to Biden and the Jan. 6 attacks on the Capitol should “follow him to his grave.”

Biden’s sweeping indictment comes in the first excerpt of “Promise Me, America,” published Monday by The Atlantic. The 46th president’s full memoir is set for a Nov. 17 release. Biden said that while doctors are encouraged by his response to cancer treatment, his activities promoting the book will be limited because of his health.

“Donald Trump led an insurrection,” Biden wrote of the attack by Trump supporters as the U.S. Congress met to certify the 2020 election won by the Democrat. “His goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office.

“The rioters weren’t ‘peaceful protesters,” he wrote. “They came armed to stop the official certification of a legitimate election.” He chided Trump for later issuing more than 1,500 pardons of the offenders.

“To this day, Trump and his supporters continue to preen and posture like they’re supporters of law enforcement,” Biden wrote. “Here’s my view: You don’t get to turn a blind eye to cops being punched, speared, sprayed, and brutalized and call yourself a friend of law enforcement. What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave.”

Biden also laments Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, especially those intended to address climate change.

“All presidents must confront a feeling that their legacy is vulnerable to the pendulum of politics and the whims of their successors,” Biden wrote. “In my case, that feeling was magnified by the dismissive and destructive nature of Donald Trump, who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down.”

The memoir’s release comes on the heels of Biden’s fellow Democrats trouncing Republicans in the midterm elections, securing stunningly broad House and Senate majorities and flipping control of several statehouses in a comprehensive rebuke of Trump’s second presidency. But Trump’s return to power two years earlier was itself a rejection of Biden’s one White House term, and many voters still harbor skeptical views of his presidency and his party.

In a lengthy social media post on Sunday, Biden pitched his memoir as the best way he can explain his presidency, “the challenges we faced, the decisions I made and why I made them.”

During his four years in office, Biden confronted the COVID-19 pandemic and its economic fallout, and he worked to restore global alliances that Trump frayed. But he faced widespread concerns about his age, and he abandoned his reelection bid after a disastrous June 2024 debate with Trump. Dogged by lingering inflation and other concerns, Biden’s vice president, Kamala Harris, lost to Trump that November.

Months after leaving office, Biden announced that he’d been diagnosed with prostate cancer. He opened up about his condition in his Sunday social media post, saying he “won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped” and urging people to let the book speak for him.

Biden said his doctors “continue to be encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment.” But, he acknowledged, “Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.”

In the excerpt, Biden recounts an unusual Oval Office meeting with Trump days after the 2020 election — well before the Jan. 6 riots.

“‘You know, Joe, if it weren’t for politics, I believe we’d be good friends,’” Trump said, according to Biden.

Trump even commented “that he’d been relieved he didn’t have to run against me,” Biden added.

Public polling at the time Biden dropped his reelection bid showed him trailing Trump, and Democrats pushed for him to yield out of fear that he could not win.

Biden said he used the meeting to give Trump “a tour of the world,” including the Ukraine-Russia war, NATO alliances, Israel and Gaza and China-U.S. relations. Biden said Trump “focused on the personalities” of world leaders rather than the substance of international relations.

He said that two-hour meeting left him worried Trump would indeed dismantle much of his presidency. He wrote that Trump’s opening weeks — his Day One executive orders and everything that followed — confirmed his worries about a “crueler government” that “tried to tear down institutions and inflame hatreds” and a president who “took a wrecking ball to our traditions.”

The memoir’s title echoes an earlier Biden book, “Promise Me, Dad,” that he wrote about his son Beau’s cancer and death — a parallel that implicitly acknowledges the former president’s age, condition and the reality that he may not have a long post-presidency to see the direction of the country and the evolution of his legacy.

In that first book, released between Biden’s vice presidency and his 2020 presidential bid, he explained that the title came directly from a father-son conversation around Thanksgiving in 2014.

“Promise me, Dad. Give me your word that no matter what happens, you’re going to be all right,” Biden recalled Beau saying. Beau Biden died six months later.

In his Sunday post, Biden repeated an argument he made often when campaigning and during his presidency, saying the U.S. is unique because it was “built on an idea” that “all of us are created equal.”

“Promise me, America,” he concluded, that “we’ll never forget it.”

news.title: Joe Biden, in White House memoir, says Trump should carry the weight of Jan. 6 riots ‘to his grave’
news.text:
ATLANTA: Former US President Joe Biden writes in his White House memoir that Donald Trump, at once his predecessor and successor, has deeply damaged the country and world with an administration determined to “tear down institutions and inflame hatreds.”

And the 83-year-old Democrat said the 80-year-old Trump’s years of lies about his 2020 defeat to Biden and the Jan. 6 attacks on the Capitol should “follow him to his grave.”

Biden’s sweeping indictment comes in the first excerpt of “Promise Me, America,” published Monday by The Atlantic. The 46th president’s full memoir is set for a Nov. 17 release. Biden said that while doctors are encouraged by his response to cancer treatment, his activities promoting the book will be limited because of his health.

“Donald Trump led an insurrection,” Biden wrote of the attack by Trump supporters as the US Congress met to certify the 2020 election won by the Democrat. “His goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office.

“The rioters weren’t ‘peaceful protesters,” he wrote. “They came armed to stop the official certification of a legitimate election.” He chided Trump for later issuing more than 1,500 pardons of the offenders.

“To this day, Trump and his supporters continue to preen and posture like they’re supporters of law enforcement,” Biden wrote. “Here’s my view: You don’t get to turn a blind eye to cops being punched, speared, sprayed, and brutalized and call yourself a friend of law enforcement. What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave.”

Biden also laments Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, especially those intended to address climate change.

“All presidents must confront a feeling that their legacy is vulnerable to the pendulum of politics and the whims of their successors,” Biden wrote. “In my case, that feeling was magnified by the dismissive and destructive nature of Donald Trump, who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down.”

Democrats won big but Biden’s reputation still lags

The memoir’s release comes on the heels of Biden’s fellow Democrats trouncing Republicans in the midterm elections, securing stunningly broad House and Senate majorities and flipping control of several statehouses in a comprehensive rebuke of Trump’s second presidency. But Trump’s return to power two years earlier was itself a rejection of Biden’s one White House term, and many voters still harbor skeptical views of his presidency and his party.

In a lengthy social media post on Sunday, Biden pitched his memoir as the best way he can explain his presidency, “the challenges we faced, the decisions I made and why I made them.”

During his four years in office, Biden confronted the COVID-19 pandemic and its economic fallout, and he worked to restore global alliances that Trump frayed. But he faced widespread concerns about his age, and he abandoned his reelection bid after a disastrous June 2024 debate with Trump. Dogged by lingering inflation and other concerns, Biden’s vice president, Kamala Harris, lost to Trump that November.

Months after leaving office, Biden announced that he’d been diagnosed with prostate cancer. He opened up about his condition in his Sunday social media post, saying he “won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped” and urging people to let the book speak for him.

Biden said his doctors “continue to be encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment.” But, he acknowledged, “Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.”

Biden tells of an unusually complimentary Trump

In the excerpt, Biden recounts an unusual Oval Office meeting with Trump days after the 2020 election — well before the Jan. 6 riots.

“‘You know, Joe, if it weren’t for politics, I believe we’d be good friends,’” Trump said, according to Biden.

Trump even commented “that he’d been relieved he didn’t have to run against me,” Biden added.

Public polling at the time Biden dropped his reelection bid showed him trailing Trump, and Democrats pushed for him to yield out of fear that he could not win.

Biden said he used the meeting to give Trump “a tour of the world,” including the Ukraine-Russia war, NATO alliances, Israel and Gaza and China-US relations. Biden said Trump “focused on the personalities” of world leaders rather than the substance of international relations.

He said that two-hour meeting left him worried Trump would indeed dismantle much of his presidency. He wrote that Trump’s opening weeks — his Day One executive orders and everything that followed — confirmed his worries about a “crueler government” that “tried to tear down institutions and inflame hatreds” and a president who “took a wrecking ball to our traditions.”

The title echoes Biden’s memoir about his late son

The memoir’s title echoes an earlier Biden book, “Promise Me, Dad,” that he wrote about his son Beau’s cancer and death — a parallel that implicitly acknowledges the former president’s age, condition and the reality that he may not have a long post-presidency to see the direction of the country and the evolution of his legacy.

In that first book, released between Biden’s vice presidency and his 2020 presidential bid, he explained that the title came directly from a father-son conversation around Thanksgiving in 2014.

“Promise me, Dad. Give me your word that no matter what happens, you’re going to be all right,” Biden recalled Beau saying. Beau Biden died six months later.

In his Sunday post, Biden repeated an argument he made often when campaigning and during his presidency, saying the US is unique because it was “built on an idea” that “all of us are created equal.”

“Promise me, America,” he concluded, that “we’ll never forget it.”
news.summary: In his upcoming memoir, Joe Biden asserts that Donald Trump bears responsibility for the Jan. 6 riots and his actions should be remembered as damaging to the nation.

news.title: Laughing My Ossoff About 2028
news.text:
Prediction market Kalshi now lists Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) as the Democrat frontrunner for 2028, and sure enough, he has become the new flavor of the month in the wake of the midterms.

The latest evidence came out of this weekend's Crooked Con convention, where a straw poll of leftist activists doubled as a referendum on the post-Kamala era. Ossoff took 38% of roughly 1,000 votes. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) finished second with 17%, and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg placed third with 14%.

2028 straw poll at Crooked Con has Ossoff first, AOC 2nd, Buttigieg 3rdAlso someone voted for Trump? pic.twitter.com/uEJGyTE9oy— Igor Bobic (@igorbobic) November 8, 2026

Everyone else landed in single digits. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro each drew 4%. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore pulled 3% apiece, and even California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who has been plotting his presidential run for years now, only managed 2.3%.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and first-term Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) have worked to raise their profiles, and both still finished under 1%. Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) collected two votes.

And Kamala? She got 0.6%, good for a 16th-place tie with Slotkin.

The party's previous vice president and 2024 nominee couldn't crack 1% in a room full of the party's most engaged activists.

Ouch again.

But I’m not here to talk about Kamala. I’m actually here to talk about Ossoff because there’s no doubt Ossoff is rising since the midterms. Unfortunately for him, he still doesn't have a chance.

To understand why, go back to 2024, when Kamala was shopping for a running mate. Rumors had her eyeing Shapiro, and Republicans had real reason to worry about a popular governor from a critical battleground state joining her ticket. I never believed she'd pick him, and the reason had nothing to do with his record or his electability.

ICYMI: Greg Gutfeld Has a Theory About the Midterms

Back in August, Bill Maher sat down with CNN's Dana Bash on his show and spoke the blunt truth about his party. "Well, in the Democratic Party, as long as that faith isn't Jewish, you're good," Maher told her. Bash, clearly caught off guard, replied, "Well, you said it." Maher held his ground. "Yeah, I said it because it's true!" he said.

Sam Markstein, national political director and spokesman for the Republican Jewish Coalition, credited Maher for his honesty. "It's a rare occasion when we agree with Bill Maher, but he's right: there is only one party where American Jews can be proudly Jewish and loudly pro-Israel, and it's the Republican Party," Markstein said. "Democrats prove it again and again — from Kamala Harris passing over Josh Shapiro in 2024 to the rise of communist elected officials who traffic in antisemitism in halls of power across the country."

He added, "The Democratic Party is being remade by its radicalized base, and party leadership continues to fecklessly whistle past the political graveyard as American Jews flee."

That brings us back to Ossoff. With socialist candidates slowly taking over the party and antisemitism now mainstream within it, he's a nonstarter. He’d never survive a primary.

news.title: Was it all about Trump? How Katie Hobbs won a second term
news.text:
Gov. Katie Hobbs stood in the backyard of a north Phoenix home, urging over 100 Democrats to help get out the vote in the final push before Election Day. She talked about what was at stake, offering a dire contrast between herself and her Republican opponent, Rep. Andy Biggs.

"He has spent the last decade in Washington, building one of the most extreme partisan records in Congress. ... Andy Biggs is also an election denier," Hobbs said. "And a pedophile," someone in the crowd shouted, a distorted version of Hobbs' message from attack advertising that Biggs dismissed as an effort at "reputational annihilation."

"We have to win this election to protect the progress that we made and protect our democracy," Hobbs said. "Donald Trump has made this election a top priority for him."

Hours later, Biggs traded his typical button-up and suit jacket for a T-shirt and headed to his regular taco spot in Gilbert. As he delivered orders, he spoke to Republicans and Democrats alike about his plans to eliminate the income tax if he were elected, convincing at least one of the latter to change her vote.

But one vote wasn't enough.

It would have taken hundreds of thousands to hold back the blue wave voters delivered in the Nov. 3 midterm, which many analysts have said was a national rebuke of President Trump's policies.

Hobbs won a second term in a blowout. As pundits prepared for vote counting to take days and Hobbs' team urged patience during that process, her race was called in a stunning 30 minutes. Democrats declared victory across the nation, flipping even once-unthinkable seats.

Hobbs, once considered one of the nation's most vulnerable Democratic incumbents, benefited from an environment that was toxic for the GOP. The office she claimed by less than 1 percentage point in 2022 will be hers again by about 13 points, as of Nov. 8, though results are still not final.

She ran a risk-averse campaign, relying on a disciplined message and amplifying Biggs' baggage with an aggressive and unrelenting advertising blitz that began within minutes of Biggs winning the GOP nomination, and continued for five months.

Biggs struggled to shift the narrative that he was far behind. Or too far right. Or a lackey for Trump. Biggs rarely put Hobbs on defense. His campaign relied on earned media coverage as major Republican donors took their money elsewhere, crippling his ability to get his pitch to voters.

Republicans' November collapse impacted governors across the nation. Democrats flipped five governors' offices away from Republicans, breaking in some cases decades-long streaks of conservative leadership. Texans had not elected a Democrat to the job since 1990. Georgians had not done so since 1998.

"The truth is, it would not have mattered what we did or what she did," Biggs' strategist Sean Noble said. "Because the tsunami was so big that there was no place to hide. There is no safe place when you have a wave at a national level of this magnitude."

"This is the easiest autopsy that you can possibly write about a campaign," he added. "And that is, Donald Trump (expletive) us."

Biggs' campaign couldn't find its message

Biggs entered the race in January 2025 at the urging of his friend, Turning Point USA co-founder Charlie Kirk. His entrance scrambled the primary race, and Biggs ultimately won with over 70% of the GOP vote in July.

His campaign threw a party in Scottsdale. But Biggs was hours late coming back from Aspen, Colorado, where he was courting the deep-pocketed Republican Governors' Association. His flight was late, and that financial lifeline never arrived.

Biggs pledged to Arizona voters that he would cut taxes and root out corruption. But he struggled to stick to his message and do so with intensity, prompting GOP allies at times to remark that Biggs wasn't aggressive enough.

A former state lawmaker and five-term congressman, Biggs had never run statewide before. After his primary in 2016, when he won by just 27 votes after a recount, he had safely won reelection in one of the state's reddest districts — an area that wasn't off limits for the midterm's blue wave. Even Biggs' daughter couldn't continue the dynasty and keep the seat red.

Biggs was a former leader of the ultra-conservative House Freedom Caucus and a top ally of Trump.

Jessica Taylor, who analyzes governors' races for The Cook Political Report, said Biggs' loss could be blamed on the national rebuke of Trump, but she also noted his caliber as a candidate. And Hobbs ran a strong campaign, she said.

"Biggs was a weaker candidate than Republicans could have run. ... But I think that when you look at the state getting a trifecta for the first time in 60 years and just the margin of the vote, certainly the national environment had something to do with it," Taylor said.

"He was so tied to Trump, and then you had his election denialism," she said. "He never was able to raise a lot of money. I think his campaign just never impressed national Republicans to an extent that they were willing to invest in the race."

Biggs didn't — and he couldn't — distance himself from a president whose approvals tanked as he implemented tariffs and launched an unpopular war in Iran.

His day job in Congress meant Biggs kept voting on Trump's controversial policies. He was one of just 32 U.S. House members who opposed a massive housing reform bill in June that passed with overwhelming, bipartisan support. Six times since the conflict began in March, Biggs voted against resolutions to end the war.

Asked about those votes, Biggs doubled down on Trump even as other Republicans were breaking ranks.

"I'm not into embarrassing the president," Biggs said in an interview in June, alleging Democrats put the resolution up for a "gotcha type of vote."

Democratic campaign attorney Roy Herrera said there was nothing Biggs' campaign could have done to win in the national environment, though better fundraising or moderating his message in the general election could have made the race more competitive. 

"It's a campaign that just never got off the ground, and it turns out now that it wouldn't have mattered if it did," Herrera said. Herrera has represented Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego's campaigns, and was the Arizona-based attorney for Joe Biden and Kamala Harris' presidential runs.

A string of general election polls universally showing Biggs trailing Hobbs scared off donors. Turning Point's political arm came to the rescue when national funders largely abandoned Biggs.

Turning Point spent over $18.5 million on advertising in the race, much of it attacking Hobbs. Some of it was on-target for voters worried about the economy, like claiming the state had lost jobs. Others seemed to be from left field: One dinged Hobbs over bad reviews when she was a professor. Turning Point also created distractions, like claiming there were "Democrats for Biggs" and forcing Biggs into a position where he was asked to name some.

Turning Point may have helped move the needle, but not enough. With just $5 million in his own bank account going into the election, Biggs couldn't staff up and the GOP grassroots began complaining when he wasn't advertising on television. His entire campaign staff was about the size of the team Hobbs hired to do communications.

And while the Republican Governors Association shifted resources to defend incumbent GOP governors in other states and open seats in much redder territory, leaving Biggs out to dry in the desert, the Democratic equivalent stepped in with its war chest and made Hobbs' reelection a top priority.

The GOP group spent over $12 million in battleground Nevada, and even that did not secure a victory. Democrat Aaron Ford ultimately knocked off incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo by almost 8 percentage points.

The Democratic Governors Association sent an estimated $23 million to Arizona to help Hobbs keep her seat.

"We brought a handshake to a nuclear war," Biggs' spokesman and senior adviser Drew Sexton said Nov. 6.

Hobbs' race at the top of the ticket

With that eight-figure outside help, Hobbs unleashed a barrage of advertising against Biggs. She spent nearly $18 million of her own fundraising stockpiled over four years and built a campaign staff early. The spending figures in this story are according to the latest reports through September, and are likely much higher.

The attacks reminded voters that Biggs blocked a bill to allow a police takeover in Colorado City, home to a corrupt polygamous cult — a scandal made worse by Biggs' shifting response. Biggs didn't have the money to combat the claims, and resorted to blaming a few of Hobbs' vetoes that he said protected sex offenders.

Other attacks said Biggs supported a bill to raise the sales tax. And that he opposed the release of the Epstein files — though Biggs pivoted in step with the president's position.

"The night Andy Biggs won the primary, we were already making the case against his record, so Arizonans heard it from us before he could introduce himself," Hobbs' campaign manager Nicole DeMont said. "That messaging defined the campaign early and exposed Biggs as incapable of answering basic questions about his record."

Hobbs' messaging almost always came back to blaming Biggs and Washington, D.C., for high costs, or tying Biggs to pedophiles.

Political observers from both parties praised Hobbs' opening salvos on the airwaves, advertisements in English and Spanish that told voters about her leadership and her own modest upbringing in Tempe — a way to relate to Arizonans frustrated by a high cost of living. Her family at times relied on food stamps. Hobbs and her husband are still paying off his student loans. The ads on television, radio and online began in May. They targeted a record-breaking audience of fans watching the FIFA World Cup, well before an election was on those voters' minds.

Hobbs, a former state lawmaker and secretary of state before she became governor, began touring the state in the fall of 2025. The stops were mostly curated events — speaking to friendly crowds. Hobbs skipped a debate, as she had four years earlier, enduring a negative news cycle but avoiding the risk of an on-stage flub.

The cautious campaign strategy turned out to be a smart one in a year of Trump turmoil.

Hobbs' campaign was clear-eyed in countering Trump's policies and rhetoric by portraying Hobbs as no-drama and the "adult in the room," said Herrera, who is not affiliated with Hobbs' campaign.

"And it ended up being exactly right," he said. "In retrospect, that's what Arizona voters tend to reward. We mostly like the kind of no-drama, the more moderate, you can say risk-averse but really more steady candidates certainly at the statewide level. That's who we tend to elect." 

The governor told voters how she had deployed the National Guard to the state's southern border. She talked about tax cuts each year she was in office and erasing medical debt for over 670,000 Arizonans. She talked about utility assistance and repealing a tax on rent.

"In 2022, Gov. Hobbs ran as a bulwark against extremism," said DeMont, who also ran Hobbs' campaign four years ago. "In 2026, she ran as a governor with a record, and we built the whole campaign around it."

And that helped Hobbs win by more than double any Democrat who ran statewide in almost 20 years, and in a state where Republican voters outnumber Democratic ones by almost 300,000, according to DeMont.

"That doesn't happen by accident," DeMont said. "It happens when Arizonans trust a governor who has delivered for them."

Choosing the former Republican mayor of Mesa, John Giles, as her running mate "told Republicans and independents there was a place for them in this campaign, and reinforced Gov. Hobbs’ approach to putting what’s best for the state over a political party," DeMont said.

'So incredibly hopeful'

Manasvi Jagtap, a 21-year-old senior at Arizona State University, said Hobbs did well in her first term. But Jagtap had friends who had not heard of Hobbs — which Jagtap believed was a good sign.

“If you hear a lot about politicians, they're usually doing something really, really crazy, either on the left side or the right side,” she said.

Jagtap said the Trump administration has done damage to the Republican Party and even more moderate conservatives were struggling to reach voters.

“Everything is just so extremely polarized that I feel people are either wanting to vote Democrat or vote for a safer option,” which would be Katie Hobbs, she said.

Marge Dillon hosted Hobbs and Kelly in her north Phoenix backyard that morning two weeks before Election Day.

Dillon, 70, is a retired educator and Arizona native who fears public schools are being "annihilated" by vouchers. She supports Hobbs' positions on public education funding and women's health issues.

"Gov. Hobbs, I think, has been a voice for those of us with the smallest voice," Dillon said. Opening her home for a get-out-the-vote event was a small thing she could do to help the candidates she prefers, Dillon said. And it happened at a pivotal time, she said.

"I think we're right on the cusp of losing democracy in America," she said on Oct. 20.

Dillon lives in a district where voters ultimately ousted incumbent Republican Sen. Shawnna Bolick in favor of Democrat Amelia Gallitano. Hobbs won the county by about 16 percentage points, according to unofficial results.

Dillon praised younger candidates and young voters who helped reelect Hobbs and pushed the state and the nation blue.

"I did not expect it to go the way that it did," she said. "I was so incredibly worried for the next generation, and now I'm so incredibly hopeful."

Reporter Erick Trevino contributed to this story.

Stacey Barchenger covers state politics. Reach her at stacey.barchenger@arizonarepublic.com or 480-416-5669.

news.title: We can’t just ‘move on’: Democrats must hold Trump accountable | Jan-Werner Müller
news.text:
Fresh from an overwhelming victory, Democrats might quickly divide over what should be seen as unnecessary fracture.

Establishment figures demand a focus on “kitchen table issues”, while others insist that successful candidates did not just campaign on the cost of living, but managed to connect people’s daily struggles with the unprecedented corruption of the Trump administration.

Indeed, Democrats have a mandate to enforce accountability. And it is imperative not to treat accountability as some kind of abstract moral question; even the most hard-headed politicians have to understand that the inability to deal with crimes and misdemeanors now will come back to haunt them – and, in fact, the nation as a whole.

Kamala Harris counseled that Democrats should concentrate on “commonsense legislation”, since the votes for impeachment simply are not there; Barack Obama has – as always – called for politicians to bring the country together.

As wise as this advice might sound, they would amount to continuing what the writer Richard Beck has called our “impunity culture”. Richard Nixon was forced to resign, but then promptly pardoned by his successor; Ronald Reagan’s Iran-Contra shenanigans never had any real consequences; after Abu Ghraib, Obama urged us to move on.

We moved on – and eventually found ourselves with Donald Trump, whose whole experience in life, business and politics has been one long morality tale about how elite figures get away with it. He has also made it a basic principle of his approach to governing that impunity can be exchanged for loyalty: after all, his underlings believe that he will pardon them before 20 January 2029.

What has happened more than once is likely to happen again. If Democrats do not find ways of holding Trumpists accountable, the message to present and future politicians will be: there are never consequences. This will also provide an incentive for those fearing the law to enter politics.

What’s more, the repercussions of impunity for Trumpists are not confined to the US: for any other government ever to trust an American administration again, there would have to be globally visible accountability, as well as a comprehensive cultural distancing from Trumpism.

Concretely: no triumphal arch or statues, golden or not, can remain standing; no foreign visitors should ever land at airports named after a president who both inspired and oversaw hitherto unknown levels of corruption (as well as cruelty).

And in the short run? Democrats can force both administration officials and associated oligarchs to testify under oath. Of particular interest would be figures who claim to be civilians, but de facto exercise state power: think Jared Kushner.

And, of course, Elon Musk. As the political scientist Dan Moynihan has pointed out, it is absurd that Elon Musk has appeared more often on Saturday Night Live than in front of Congress to talk about Doge; the country needs answers about what his vandals did in 2025, whether they stole and weaponized data, and how exactly his companies remain untangled with the American state – creating a kind of dependency on one person that, as Ukraine discovered already, is incompatible with any kind of responsible governance.

As in the last years of the first Trump administration, those called to testify might simply ignore the invitation to the Hill. Democrats can go to court, and they will win, but all that takes time.

The policy scholar Norm Ornstein has suggested the Capitol police should simply capture recalcitrant individuals and hold them at the Capitol. That is legally possible and even has precedents; but it is unlikely to happen (though it would also provide a symbolic closure of the period that began with Maga hordes assaulting Congress on 6 January 2021).

Direct legal consequences are also unlikely, as long as the Department of Justice sees itself as merely an extension of the president’s will. Many lawyers have left; the sycophants who replaced them are often unqualified, and, in any case, unwilling to do anything about rampant corruption and criminality.

That leaves impeachment. While the votes might not be there in the Senate, Democrats could start to go after the most egregious cabinet members – Hegseth and Robert F Kennedy Jr might compete for the top of the list.

Impeachment has a political purpose – it is meant to prevent further damage to the Republic – but it can also serve a pedagogical function. It shows citizens the evidence for crimes and misdemeanors, and that evidence, carefully assembled, can then eventually also be helpful to a Department of Justice that has regained its integrity.

If nothing else, the country, just like societies emerging from authoritarianism elsewhere in the world, will need a precise record of what happened, for a sense of closure, if nothing else.

Republicans will cry “weaponization” – again. But that simply shows that they are unwilling to entertain any limits on the behavior of their leader and what must be called his extended mafia state.

And, who knows, some Republican senators might jump ship when confronted with the question of whether they still support a secretary of defense, who has done enormous damage to US military power.

Self-declared moderates among the Democrats will say that precious political capital and public attention should not be squandered on issues which have no impact on people’s day-to-day lives.

But this profoundly underestimates citizens’ desire for justice; it also fails to see that, with a large majority in the House, one can do more than one thing. As Raphael Warnock keeps reminding his party, one can walk and chew gum at the same time.

 Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton University

The new Congress cannot maintain the culture of political impunity that got us here in the first place
