news.title: What Gavin Newsom’s mass commutation says about death penalty politics
news.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s announcement on Nov. 5 of a universal clemency for the 548 people awaiting execution in his state marks an important turning point in American politics. It signals the end of law-and-order politics as a determining factor in the calculations of likely presidential contenders.

Newsom, an ambitious politician who is almost certain to run for president in 2028, reportedly weighed the impact that commuting hundreds of death sentences — including those of some notorious killers — would have on his political prospects.

That Newsom went ahead with the mass clemency tells us a lot about the salience of tough-on-crime positions in the present political moment. Opposition to capital punishment is no longer the death knell for people aspiring to be president.

This is not to say that Newsom won’t face backlash, either in California or elsewhere in the country, for his clemency decision. As the New York Times notes, “Those against Mr. Newsom’s move are expected to file a challenge arguing that he violated the law with a blanket commutation and that each case must be considered on individual merits.”

The Times reports that “Marc Klaas, the father of Polly Klaas, whose kidnapping and murder prompted an era of tough-on-crime policies in California, is livid at the idea of Mr. Newsom granting mercy to his daughter’s killer, or anyone else sentenced to death.” Klaas told the Times that he was aghast at Newsom “putting his energy” into commuting the death sentences of “serial killers, spree killers, cop killers, baby killers. We’re talking about absolutely the worst people in our society, without a doubt.”

“The act,” the Times continues, “could make him [Newsom] a more compelling candidate to liberal voters in a Democratic primary, but likely would open him to attacks in a general election.”

But Newsom’s opposition to capital punishment was already baked into his political brand. He had been very public in stating his view that it is immoral, and in taking dramatic anti-capital punishment actions, like imposing a moratorium on executions in his state in 2019.

Moreover, fear of crime is no longer a driving force in the way Americans vote. When voters in this week’s midterms were asked to rank six issues in order of importance, crime came in dead last, with only 3% of people surveyed saying it was the most important issue facing the country.

In 1988 a group supporting then-Vice President George H.W. Bush created the the so-called Willie Hoton ad to brand his Democratic opponent, then-Massachusetts Gov. Michael Dukakis, as soft on crime. That ad put the death penalty front and center. 

We need only look back to the 2024 presidential campaign, when Donald Trump took every opportunity to stoke fears of crime. Yet only 1% of the electorate said crime was the most important issue in their decision about whom to vote for as president.

Also recall that in 2020, every candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination but one publicly opposed the death penalty, and with his election Joe Biden became the first president to advocate ending capital punishment.

That would have seemed unimaginable several decades ago. In 1988 a group supporting then-Vice President George H.W. Bush created the the so-called Willie Hoton ad to brand his Democratic opponent, then-Massachusetts Gov. Michael Dukakis, as soft on crime. That ad put the death penalty front and center. It started by stating that Bush supported the death penalty and Dukakis opposed it.

As a 2015 report on WNYC explained, “The Willie Horton ad had implications that stretched far beyond the 1988 campaign season — it ultimately pushed a button of fear that marked the beginning of a ‘tough on crime’ era.”

For example, during the 1992 campaign, then-Arkansas Gov. Bill Clinton was so determined to forestall a similar attack that he briefly left the campaign trail in New Hampshire to fly back to his home state to preside over an execution. As a 2015 article in The Atlantic observed, “State law did not require the governor's presence, but politics did: Clinton wanted to raise his national profile and reverse the Democratic Party's soft-on-crime image.”

That Newsom could afford to do what Dukakis and Clinton could not is of enormous significance for our politics.

As was the case eight years ago, he will not be alone in opposing the death penalty if he seeks the Democratic nomination for president. Among others rumored to run, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro called for the abolition of capital punishment in February 2023. Shapiro recounted his own evolution on that issue. “I ran for attorney general twice in support of the death penalty in the most heinous of cases,” he said. “And then when those cases would reach my desk, more and more, I found that I was unable to pursue capital punishment.”

Georgia Sen. Jon Osoff has long been vocal in calling for the death penalty’s end. He is a co-sponsor of a bill that would end the federal death penalty.

Another possible rival for the Democratic nomination, former Vice President Kamala Harris, said in 2019, “I’ve long been opposed to the death penalty. It is deeply immoral, irreversible, and ineffective … This failed system is immoral, and as President I would lead the fight to end it. It’s simply the right thing to do.”

In the end, Newsom did the right thing when he extended mercy to everyone with a death sentence in California. And he is unlikely to pay much of a political price for doing so.

news.title: The 5 most consequential developments from a jaw-dropping election
news.text:
The nation's biggest political shift in a half-century sparked a flood of jaw-dropping headlines.

Democrats take control of the House and Senate, winning even in such deep red states as Kansas and South Carolina. Electoral breakthroughs for candidates who are Black, Hispanic, Native American and gay. A Democratic socialist elected mayor in the nation's second-largest city, Los Angeles, joining one elected last year in the largest, New York.

With the final votes now being counted from the Nov. 3 midterm elections, here are five of the most jaw-dropping developments of all − and ones with the biggest potential to have lasting repercussions ahead.

Most seismic shift by a state: Texas

Texas Democrats, who had not won a statewide elected office since 1994, carried all of them.

Gina Hinojosa ousted Greg Abbott, the nation's longest-serving governor, and newcomer James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton, a fixture in Texas politics. Democratic candidates won races for lieutenant governor, attorney general, comptroller, land commissioner, agriculture commissioner and railroad commissioner, and they claimed seven statewide judicial elections, including four seats on the state's Supreme Court.

It was a Texas-sized sweep.

The swing was stunning among Latino voters, who make up nearly a third of the state's eligible voters.

Hispanics who had swung to Donald Trump in 2024 snapped back to Democrats, especially in the Rio Grande Valley and other Texas border counties. That trend was nationwide: In exit polls sponsored by NBC News and other news organizations, Democrats carried Latinos by 30 percentage points, 64%-34%.

If Democrats can succeed in making the Lone Star State blue or even purple, that could have seismic repercussions for the calculations on how to carry the White House in 2028.

Among the four biggest states, Democrats have generally relied on California and New York while Republicans have counted on Florida and Texas.

It's been 50 years since Texas backed a Democrat for president. If it's no longer reliably red, the Electoral College could face its most fundamental realignment since then.

Most seismic shift by a voter group: Young people

In the 2024 presidential race, Trump scored major gains for a Republican among voters under 30, who had been a Democratic-leaning group. He split them about evenly with Democrat Kamala Harris and carried a majority of young men.

But they didn't stick with the GOP the next time around. In the midterms, more than 7 of 10 younger voters cast their ballots for Democratic House candidates.

Notably, that included more than 6 in 10 younger voters who are White, a demographic that Trump had won by 10 points. And nearly 6 in 10 younger men, a reversal after Trump had carried 56% of them in 2024.

To be sure, young people were as usual less likely to vote than their elders. They made up just over 10% of the midterm electorate.

But their loyalty is clearly up for grabs − and they will be around to vote for decades more.

Biggest unintended consequence: Louisiana v. Callais

In April, the Supreme Court significantly limited the 1965 Voting Rights Act, allowing Louisiana to adopt a redistricting map that eliminated one of the state's two majority-Black congressional districts. By 6-3, a conservative majority set a new and higher standard for triggering the law's provisions, designed to protect minority voting rights.

In a dissent, Justice Elena Kagan warned that the decision left a key section of the Voting Rights Act "all but a dead letter," and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund called it "devastating."

But dismay over the decision ended up creating what has been dubbed a "blacklash," intensifying efforts by Black candidates and activists. In the midterms, Black governors were elected for the first time in Florida, Georgia, Nevada and Wisconsin.

That's more than the total number of Black governors elected ever − there have been three − and it included the first gubernatorial election ever of a Black woman, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia.

Most startling surprise: Mississippi

Only two U.S. Senate races hadn't been called as of Nov. 8. One was in Alaska, which was expected to be close.

The other was in Mississippi. Which wasn't.

With 97% of the vote counted, Democrat Scott Colom led Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by 49.1%-48.8%, a margin of 2,574 votes. That gives Colom a narrow lead but not a guaranteed victory.

It's been more than a decade since any Democrat won statewide office in Mississippi.

And it's been more than 150 years, since Reconstruction, since a Black candidate won statewide office there.

Shortest-lived voter coalition: Trump 2024

The coalition that sent Trump back to the White House two years ago has fractured.

In 2024, with an electorate dissatisfied with President Joe Biden's leadership, especially on inflation, Trump made major gains among crucial voter groups. They included Black men and moderates as well as Hispanics and young people.

Voters are still dissatisfied on inflation and most are opposed to the war in Iran, which has driven up the price of fuel and more. Exit polls gave Trump a job-approval rating of 37% at the midterms, lower than Biden's job-approval rating of 41% on the eve of the 2024 election, which his vice president lost.

That's not the first time that declarations of a new governing coalition proved short-lived. Republicans predicted a realignment after George W. Bush's reelection in 2004, and Democrats did the same after Barack Obama's election in 2008.

But Bush was succeeded by Obama, then Obama by Trump as voters sought change.

"The American people clearly want change that's bold, change that's transformational and change that is dramatic," House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, the likely new House speaker, said on ABC's "This Week." "And that's everywhere."

"So I think even though the Democrats had a big night on Tuesday, that does not mean that the country is now all supportive of all the Democrat policies," Florida governor-elect Byron Donalds, a Republican, cautioned on NBC's "Meet the Press."

The question for Democrats now: Can they succeed in building a more durable coalition?

news.title: Joe Biden to scale back book tour as cancer ‘slows me down’
news.text: Former President Joe Biden signaled he will have to scale back the tour to promote his upcoming memoir “Promise me, America,” as he continues to undergo treatment for cancer. “Some days are better than others,” Biden wrote in a lengthy post on X on Sunday. “It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.” As a result, Biden said he would no longer “be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped. However, I’m hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves.” Months after leaving office in January 2025, Biden, 83, announced that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer and has since undertaken courses of radiation therapy and hormone treatment. Last year, his office also shared that he had undergone surgery to remove cancerous skin cells. The memoir is due out on Nov. 17 and details his four years in the White House, including “the decisions I made, and why I made them,” he wrote. “More than anything, it’s about my faith in the American people and the great American experiment in self-governance and democracy.” In August, his son, Hunter Biden, told the BBC in an interview that his father’s cancer had spread to other parts of his body and was causing him pain, even as he continues to speak out on public issues. “The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” Hunter Biden told the BBC in August. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects.” “It’s really sad to watch,” he added. Former first lady Jill Biden also previously told NBC News: “I think Joe will live with cancer till the rest of his life.” Biden was the oldest man to serve as U.S. president and his age and health were a source of concern for much of his time in office. The memoir of the 46th president delves into “his campaign, his presidency, his decision to run again,” according to the publisher, Hachette Book Group. It also “reveals the deeply agonizing calculation behind his decision in the summer of 2024 to step aside from the presidential race and to put his party and the nation before his personal ambitions.” Biden suspended that re-election bid and ultimately endorsed his vice president, Kamala Harris, after mounting pressure to step aside. Biden has frequently defended himself against accusations about his mental acuity and memory. Biden said in the post Sunday that his doctors were “encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment,” and thanked the public for their prayers and well wishes as he vowed to keep fighting.
news.summary: Former President Joe Biden said his tour to promote his presidential memoir “Promise me, America,” will be scaled back, as he continues to battle cancer.

news.title: Election 2026: Reflections on the Deep Blue Victories
news.text:
Election 2026 is over, and it didn’t go well. Final tallies are still trickling in for California (they always do), but those elections are a foregone conclusion. The AP called the California governor’s race at the closing of the polls, and I am too jaded by liberal Californians’ repeated votes for failure to scream about voter fraud. No matter how much fraud there may be, I have witnessed enough town halls and political discourse in this state to recognize that Californians are afflicted with Republican Derangement Syndrome and Trump Derangement Syndrome in particular.

Perennial politician and policy nonentity Xavier Becerra is the governor-elect. He crumbled in debates, then hid from voters and reporters during the campaign season. In contrast, Republican Fox News host-turned-populist author Steve Hilton campaigned everywhere, in heavily Democrat areas as well as Republican strongholds. Hilton hustled; he had good ideas; he even posted advertisements on major freeways (unheard of for a Republican candidate), yet he still fell short.

Across the country, Democrats made unprecedented gains in ruby-red states. These states have election integrity measures and voter protections. Democrats swamped the vote and won fair and square.

Sure, my predictions were wrong, but hope has to take that risk. I choose to be optimistic about every election, no matter how daunting the odds. No matter how severe the odds or how disappointing the losses, I have learned to persevere, and hopefully the country will, as well. We survived Joe Biden, and voters rejected Kamala Harris in 2024 to give Trump a second mandate.

Then what happened? Trump rode a wave of strong support at the outset of his second term. Americans wanted a return to order, and he reversed the damage of the Biden years. Two years later, voters have given congressional power to the woke Democrats committed to the cults of climate change, transgenderism, and socialism.

Did high gas prices and inflation so embitter American voters that they would allow woke communists to take power? Sadly, yes. They should have looked past the high gas prices and reflected on President Trump’s accomplishments: record job creation, mass deportations, lower rents, protection of life and family, and restored prestige for the American military and the American experiment.

Regarding the war in Iran, President Trump did the right thing in targeting that rogue regime’s nuclear enrichment program. The United States would have stood helpless against an Islamic nuclear holocaust, along with the rest of the civilized world, if the Ayatollahs and the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps had established an impenetrable wall of missiles to protect their nuclear enrichment. Since Jimmy Carter, no president has wanted to take on and take down the fanatical, megalomaniacal Islamic regime. Trump showed the necessary political courage.

If Republicans suffered because Trump put America First by taking out the world’s biggest geopolitical threat, so be it. I reject the dismissive commentary of Matt Walsh, who declared: “I'd rather Iran have a nuke than my country be run by communists.” Can’t we have both? We should seek both outcomes, and we should not disparage Trump for doing the right thing, even if he didn’t get the messaging right or struggled to corral other Republicans to focus on more domestic victories.

What other lessons can we draw from this midterm mess?

 1. Let’s start with a lighter note: Guam’s results are not indicative of the election results to come across the country. I was so hopeful yesterday afternoon when I read Trump’s announcement about our little territory far away in the Pacific Ocean.

In 2022, a Republican won the Congressional delegate seat, the first time in 30 years, yet Republicans enjoyed only a red trickle across the rest of the country. In 2026, Republicans won Guam’s governor’s race, but the results were even worse for Republicans elsewhere. 

Guam’s election results were not a perfect harbinger by any means. Lesson learned.

 2. Republicans in red states took their longstanding dominance for granted, and voters are tired of it. Iowa, Texas, and Ohio turned blue this season, after years of Republican rule in the legislature and statewide offices, because they were angry with the lack of results at the state level. Some candidates were so damaged, like Ken Paxton, or had so upset the Republican base, like Vivek Ramaswamy, that Republican voters did not turn out for them.

Mississippi’s U.S. Senate seat is trending Democrat, as well: unthinkable to some, but I have followed statewide election trends in the Magnolia State, and the Republican gubernatorial candidates have been winning by diminishing margins. Corruption issues and lack of conservative legislative success have outraged voters there, too.

 3. Republican voters feel betrayed by Trump, and they took it out on his party. Whether those feelings are justified is another story, but telling people “Everything is fine” while they face rising costs is not a winning electoral strategy. Then again, Trump’s leadership has been nothing but winning, even if congressional Republicans didn’t step up.

What are the silver linings to the Republican Election Disaster of 2026?

 1. My favorite executive, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, is the biggest winner. Throughout his excellent and effective tenure, he committed himself to policy goals and gains, no matter what happened in Washington. He made promises, he kept them, and turned Florida into a Republican stronghold so stable that Republicans carried all statewide offices this year despite the blue tsunami. Governor-elect Byron Donalds owes him a great deal. Voters want results and a mission, not memes and noise, and DeSantis delivered. He is a strong contender for 2028 now, despite MAGA naysayers offended by his 2024 primary challenge.

 2. Idaho’s abortion initiative, Proposition One, failed despite the motivated liberal turnout on Election Day. Conservative values can withstand and win against unfavorable political environments. The pro-life movement mobilized early to fight this horrid attempt to enshrine abortion rights in the Gem State, and they succeeded. This is a huge win because abortion measures had been passing around the country up to now.

 3. Voter ID and “Citizen Voter Only” initiatives won big across the country, despite Democrats replacing Republicans in GOP strongholds. President Trump’s efforts to secure the vote should not be scuttled or dismissed. Republicans need to focus on these popular issues and accomplish them!

 4. Initiatives to protect women’s sports from confused men have won in Arizona and Nebraska, and they are winning even in deep-blue Colorado. Even Washington State’s initiative to keep boys out of girls’ sports is succeeding. This is great!

 5. In uber-liberal California, voters rejected the awful Millionaire’s Tax, Proposition 40, with the help of massive donations from wealthy job creators who would have fled the state if it passed. Voters also supported Proposition 42 to protect savings and other property from taxes. When there’s no partisan messaging but a clear commitment to doing what is best for voters, good initiatives can succeed in California.

Democrats may have won big this year, but not because their ideas are great. Republicans need to make MAGA happen consistently, not just talk about it. Am I worried for the future? No. Democrats in Congress and across the country will overplay their hand, and Republicans will capitalize on their failures to surge back in 2028.

news.title: Democrats’ New Plan to Bypass the Electoral College
news.text:
Among the many regrettable outcomes of last week’s midterm elections is a significant increase in the number of states in which Democrats gained governing trifectas. Specifically, they took control of state legislatures and governorships in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin, and Nevada. Combined with the 18 states the Democrats controlled before the midterms, this means they theoretically have the power to nullify the Electoral College by joining the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC). For those unfamiliar with NPVIC, it’s a Democratic scheme to change the way we elect presidents without messing with that pesky constitutional amendment process. 

How would NPVIC achieve this miracle? Pursuant to a formal agreement among states controlling 270 or more presidential electors, each member of the compact would be required to cast all of its electoral votes for the candidate who wins the national popular vote — without regard to the winner of the popular vote in any single state. For instance, if NPVIC had been in effect during the 2024 presidential election a member state like Colorado would have been forced to cast its 10 electoral votes for Donald Trump, despite the fact that Kamala Harris won the Centennial State by double digits. Yet its advocates insist NPVIC would be more democratic than the Electoral College:

The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would guarantee the Presidency to the candidate who receives the most popular votes across all 50 states and the District of Columbia … The winner-take-all method of awarding electoral votes repeatedly generates controversies over real or imagined irregularities and incentivizes hair-splitting litigation. A mere 537 popular votes in one state decided the national outcome in 2000. An average of only about 280,000 popular votes spread over one, two, or three closely divided states decided the last seven presidential elections. In contrast, the national-popular-vote lead averaged 4,327,902 votes over the last seven.

If all five of the states listed above decide to join NPVIC, then the total number of electoral votes controlled by the compact’s members would increase to 283, thirteen more than the 270 its members claim they need to bypass the Electoral College. The 18 states that have already joined NPVIC are the usual suspects: California (54), Colorado (10), Connecticut (7), Delaware (3), Hawaii (4), Illinois (19), Maine (4), Maryland (10), Massachusetts (11), Minnesota (10), New Jersey (14), New Mexico (5), New York (28), Oregon (8), Rhode Island (4), Vermont (3), Virginia (13), Washington (12), and the District of Columbia (3). These 23 states would, according to the stipulations of NPVIC, choose the president without the consent of the other 27 states or their voters.

It isn’t clear that the remaining 27 states will be inclined to accept being locked out of the presidential selection process without challenging the constitutionality of NPVIC. And it isn’t difficult to guess on what grounds they would base a challenge. Article I, Section 10, Clause 3 of the Constitution states the following: “No State shall, without the Consent of Congress … enter into any Agreement or Compact with another State.” Because the Democrats will control both Houses of Congress, they will be far friendlier to NPVIC than the current Congress, but they won’t have a filibuster-proof majority of 60 votes in the Senate. And, as Cato Institution’s Paul E. Godek writes, NPVIC will force some member states to disenfranchise their own voters.

First, joining the NPVIC means that the assignment of a state’s electoral votes in a future election will not be in accordance with the will of the majority of the state’s voters. That outcome is, indeed, the explicit method of the NPVIC. If the winner of a state’s popular vote is the loser of the national popular vote, then the electors will be allocated contrary to the majority of that state’s voters. By joining the NPVIC, therefore, a state commits itself to disenfranchising its own voters, nullifying their votes in some future election. Disenfranchisement would seem to violate the plain text of the Constitution, which guarantees the vote to all eligible citizens. CheckVoting Info

All of this can be avoided if the Democrats were truly interested in “one person, one vote.” It could be accomplished without NPVIC. The states could pursue genuine reform by simply choosing to allocate their electoral votes proportionally. Nebraska and Maine have already changed their allocation systems to something approximating this method, and it involves no conflict with the Constitution. It would, however, reduce the enormous electoral power wielded by the largest Democratic states. In California, which contains the largest number of Republicans of any other state, more than 20 of its 54 electoral votes would go to the “Grand Old Party.”

This is why no Democrat-controlled state would dream of going to a fully proportional system. It is why they have concocted the unconstitutional and undemocratic National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. They aren’t interested in genuine electoral reform, and the claim that NPVIC is a “conservative compromise” doesn’t pass the laugh test. They want to shift more power to heavily populated, Democrat-dominated regions and keep the electoral advantage they already possess in large states like California, New York, and now even Texas. NPVIC is, in the final analysis, just another Democrat scheme to rig the game. It’s just what they do.

news.title: Democrats promised to fix the economy. What can they really do?
news.text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio—Tom Green had a wish list when he cast his vote in the Democratic Party’s midterm landslide last week: Tougher rules on AI data centers. Universal healthcare. Better job protections.

The 29-year-old software engineer helped elect Sherrod Brown to the Senate and Amy Acton to the governor’s office. Both Democrats pledged to stop energy-hungry AI data centers from raising consumers’ electricity bills. Brown aims to cap utility rate increases and control prescription-drug prices. Acton promises to forgive medical debt and deliver tax breaks to families.

The voters who powered the Democrats’ triumph in the midterms delivered a blunt message: Make the economy work for us. Now, Democrats must deliver.

Whether they can isn’t assured, despite the party’s pending control of the House and Senate. Many demands are beyond the reach of lawmakers to fix. The main tools of Congress, taxes and spending, are limited and slow-moving—and lawmakers still face Trump’s veto.

The new majority may struggle to stop the war in Iran, which has driven up energy prices in the months since President Trump’s decision to attack. Gasoline prices, largely set by global energy markets, could remain high even if the war ends.

In the Senate, Democrats are teeing up votes to repeal Trump’s tariffs on Canada, part of his global trade war that has contributed to rising prices. Yet they acknowledge that stricter limits to presidential tariff authority—which Trump has taken to its limits worldwide—could be vetoed and would likely have to wait for another administration.

View full Image
A highway billboard in Madison Heights, Mich., referencing higher gas prices.

Satisfying voter wishes also could have unintended consequences. Curbing data centers and slowing AI, for instance, might dent the U.S. economy, harming many of the same voters who want to rein them in. The Nasdaq plunged on Thursday, driven by investor fears that the new Democratic-controlled Congress will crush the AI boom that has powered the markets.

One of the first goals for House Democrats is reversing Trump’s cuts to Medicaid and Affordable Care Act subsidies, which were part of last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill, said Rep. Debbie Dingell (D., Mich.). She is huddling with fellow lawmakers about ranking their legislative priorities. “We’re going to have a 100-hour agenda, and a 100-day agenda” after Democrats take control of Congress on Jan. 3, Dingell said in an interview.

Expanding benefits, while providing immediate relief to struggling households, could goose inflation in the longer term, as well as add to the deficit if not offset with higher taxes.

The U.S. economy’s overall strength has failed to change the glum mood of Americans who are sharing little in its growth. A larger share of America’s growing national income has gone to investors, not to employees. The Labor Department reported that the proportion of economic output going to workers in salary and benefits is at its smallest share in data that go back 80 years.

Borrowing costs are high and, with mortgage rates around 7%, many would-be home buyers are locked out of a prized piece of the American dream. Those rates are heavily influenced by moves from the Federal Reserve, which raises rates to tamp down inflation or lowers them to boost employment. Right now, inflation is the problem, not unemployment, and investors expect rates to move higher.

Over the past three months, the U.S. has added an average of 137,000 jobs a month, and unemployment has remained low. Yet, hiring has cooled compared with past years, and millions of Americans can’t find full-time employment in their fields.

View full Image
Ohio voter Tom Green.

Green, the Ohio voter, was laid off from his $89,000-a-year job as a software engineer at a bank seven months ago. After sending out 500 résumés, he has been invited to only a dozen interviews—a common complaint among job seekers. He put his home-buying plans on hold and, without healthcare coverage, pays cash for his medications.

“The economy doesn’t seem great, at least from my perspective,” said Green, a Democrat.

‘Everything went up’

Democratic state lawmakers and elected officials around the U.S. might have more leeway than their congressional counterparts to set new policies on housing, wages, taxes and data-center development. Democrats won control of the governor’s seat and both houses of the state legislature in at least six states, including Michigan, Arizona and Nevada.

Newly elected Democratic governors Gina Hinojosa in Texas, Acton in Ohio, and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia all campaigned on restricting data centers.

In Michigan, Jocelyn Benson successfully ran for governor on promises to lower costs, raise wages and end corruption. Benson plans to pass a $5,000 tax credit for caregivers, expand medical debt relief and establish a prescription-drug affordability board with the authority to approve price increases. Benson also wants to guarantee teachers a minimum starting salary of $60,000 a year, she said.

Simple math explains why affordability became a driving force in the midterm election. Inflation was 3.7% for the 12 months through September, lifted by surging gasoline prices from the Iran war, tariffs and price spikes tied to the AI boom, according to the Labor Department. Through October, average earnings rose 3.1%.

“For politicians, if you can make real wages rise consistently, that’s your path to victory and success,” said Don Schneider, a former economic adviser to congressional Republicans now at investment bank Piper Sandler. Relative to incomes, he said, prices have been rising “too fast for things that are really important to voters, like groceries and going out to dinner.”

View full Image
Voters casting ballots at a grocery store in Lawrence, Kan.

There are two paths to help workers keep up with rising prices. One that Democrats have discussed is through higher minimum wages or making it easier for workers to form unions and gain more bargaining power.

The other path is lowering inflation so that price increases steal less of household paychecks. Beyond Democrats’ efforts to repeal tariffs and end the war in Iran, some economists argue for shrinking the federal budget deficit to lower inflation.

In Delaware County, Ohio, two friends, Kim Bell and Tiffany Weiser, said they backed Democrats partly in hopes they would end tariffs and help bring down the cost of groceries and other goods. Weiser, 51, said she gave up on renovating her front porch this summer because “the cost of wood and everything went up so much just from last summer.”

Democrats’ leverage to pass legislation is now increased because Republican survivors of the midterm rout will likely be more open to working with the majority, said Jared Bernstein, who was a top economic adviser to former President Joe Biden.

“I think a potentially impactful outcome of this election is the recognition by Republicans that tying your future to Trump is a losing strategy,” Bernstein said. “If that’s the case, I could perhaps see Republicans joining with Democrats on affordability issues.”

View full Image
Democrat Senate winner Sherrod Brown celebrating at an election party in Columbus, Ohio.

Michael Faulkender, who served as deputy Treasury secretary in the Trump administration last year, said that legislation now moving through Congress to streamline the permitting process for energy projects and other infrastructure shows the two parties can find some common ground on economic measures. The latest version of the bill, which could ease energy prices by boosting supply, represents a deal between Senate Republicans and Democrats.

“If you look at who negotiated the permitting reform, there’s quite a bit of ideological breadth,” Faulkender said. “It shows we can come to a compromise.”

High stakes

Even with a strong mandate, Democrats in Congress will have limited power to quickly make America more affordable.

The most powerful tool for fighting inflation belongs to Fed policymakers, who raised their benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point in September, pushing up borrowing costs. Many investors expect another increase next month, although they have recently pared back their bets on how high the Fed might bring rates next year.

David Conklin, a 61-year-old in Delaware County, Ohio, was a Democrat for many years but voted for an independent candidate during the 2024 presidential election because he didn’t like Trump or former Vice President Kamala Harris.

View full Image
David Conklin outside his polling place in Sunbury, Ohio.

In the midterm election, he swung back to the Democrats to vote for Brown and Acton. He said he was motivated partly by Brown’s pledge to curb data-center construction. He also wants Democrats to end the war in Iran, but he isn’t sure they can.

Democrats will control both chambers next year, but Trump can veto legislation. Most bills require 60 votes to overcome a Senate filibuster, a tactic used to stall legislation. Democrats have so far won 54 Senate seats, and votes are still being tabulated for two others.

“I think it’s going to be really tough to move the needle,” said Sarah Bianchi, a strategist at Evercore ISI who held senior economic roles in the Obama and Biden administrations. “They don’t have 60 votes, and they have the president, who’s not going to sign everything. Even if those weren’t constraints, making things more affordable is actually really hard.”

Matt Molyneux, a 47-year-old handyman for commercial properties in the Davenport, Iowa, area, didn’t like cuts that Republicans made to the social safety net. Molyneux’s finances are in good shape now, he said. In the past, he said, he received food stamps and understands how important they are. That is what prompted him to vote after sitting out elections since 2020.

“I was one of those people, at one point in time, and I needed that help,” he said. “I want to make sure that keeps going.”

Christina Bohannan, one of the Democrats Molyneux voted for, said in an interview that reversing those cuts should be a priority for the new Congress. Voters shared their cost-of-living worries during her House campaign, she said.

“The Medicaid cuts are going to have potentially catastrophic effects on our hospitals here in Iowa,” said Bohannan, who expects some Republican lawmakers to support restoring the funds.

Some newly elected Democrats know firsthand how quickly they can lose their posts if they don’t deliver on their promises.

In 2022, Republican Jen Kiggans told voters in southeastern Virginia that she had a plan to fight inflation and lower the cost of living. They voted her into office that year and fired two-term Rep. Elaine Luria, a Democrat. On Tuesday, voters gave Luria her old job back.

That roller-coaster ride through four congressional campaigns has sharpened Luria’s understanding of the stakes, especially when it comes to pocketbook issues.

“Republicans broke their promises,” Luria said after her win last week. “I took back my seat from someone who went to Congress promising a lot of things, but who backed policies that made people’s lives a lot harder.”

Green, the Ohio voter, said he was counting on promises by Abdul El-Sayed, the newly elected Democratic senator from Michigan, to back Medicare for All, a single-payer national health insurance system. Republicans are dead-set against it.

“There has to be evidence that changes are being made or attempts at changes are being made,” Green said. Otherwise, he added, “I’m afraid the electorate will swing right back.”

news.title: Democrats, Please Take Note: Peace Is Good Politics
news.text:
Voters across the United States were loud and clear on Tuesday in their historic drubbing of Trumpism. The election was a decisive rejection of Trump’s war on Iran and its staggering costs at home. While savoring their victory and the historic opportunity to restore America’s constitutional order, the Democrats should take the anti-war message of the election to heart, because they suffered the same verdict two years ago, when voters rejected the Biden administration’s wars in Ukraine and Gaza. Last week Israeli voters rejected Netanyahu’s reckless wars, and European voters are also rejecting parties that prolong the Ukraine War. The message of voters is the same everywhere: diplomacy is safer, more effective, and trillions of dollars cheaper than war.

On election night Trump conceded to Fox News, “I think a part of it was Iran.” The next day Vice President JD Vance was far blunter, posting on X: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night… everyone knows why we lost.” In the AP Voter Poll, about 60 percent of voters said the decision to use military force against Iran was wrong, and about 90 percent called the cost of living a crucial or major factor in their vote.

The war and the cost of living were of course utterly intertwined. Gasoline prices, around $2.80 per gallon before the war began on February 28, had risen by about 55 percent by mid-May and reached a monthly average of $4.43 in September. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed from below 4 percent before the war to above 5 percent in the autumn, and the Pentagon sought more than $200 billion in supplemental war funding. Every family with a mortgage, a car loan or a credit card balance suffered from the war.

Voters everywhere are sending the same message: peace through diplomacy.

The first duty of the new Congress is to restore its constitutional authority over war and its power of the purse to ensure that US forces are not sent back into combat in Iran or anywhere else on the whim of a president and the behest of domestic or foreign lobbies. Trump must of course refrain from restarting the war, which was never remotely necessary or justified. Remember that on February 28, the day the US and Israel launched the war, Oman’s foreign minister, who was mediating the U.S.-Iran talks, had said that a deal was within reach.

The Democrats should not imagine that the anti-war lesson applies only to Republicans. Kamala Harris lost in 2024 because voters held the Biden administration responsible for the costs of its own wars. The energy shock that followed the escalation of the Ukraine war in 2022 drove up inflation, and gasoline topped $5 per gallon for the first time in June 2022. Biden twice rejected negotiations that could have ended the conflict: in December 2021, when his administration refused to negotiate on NATO enlargement in response to Russia’s draft security treaty, and in April 2022, when the Istanbul talks were abandoned at the behest of the US and UK.

The Gaza genocide also cost the Democrats directly. Among Americans who voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but not for Harris in 2024, 29 percent named ending Israel’s violence in Gaza as the main factor in their decision, the most frequently cited issue. The party’s voters have moved far ahead of its leaders. A New York Times/Siena poll in May 2026 found that roughly three-quarters of Democratic voters oppose US military and economic assistance to Israel.

Voters everywhere are sending the same message: peace through diplomacy. On October 27, after Israeli wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, Netanyahu lost his majority. Similarly, European leaders who have tied themselves to open-ended war in Ukraine are being rejected by the voters. Only 10 percent of Germans are satisfied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, the lowest rating ever recorded for a German chancellor. Emmanuel Macron’s approval fell to 15 percent in October. In Bulgaria, Iliana Iotova, who favors dialogue with Moscow, won the presidency on November 1 with more than 58 percent of the vote.

A key upcoming key test for the Democrats will be Ukraine. They must stop their party’s typical Russia-bashing and instead support a diplomatic end to the war.

As a start, the Democrats should remember why the war started. In 1990 the United States assured Mikhail Gorbachev that NATO would not move “one inch eastward.” The Clinton administration broke that promise. In 2008 the Bush administration pushed through the Bucharest declaration that Ukraine and Georgia “will become members of NATO,” despite Ambassador William Burns’s warning that this was the brightest of all red lines for Russia. In 2014 the United States backed the coup against Ukraine’s elected president, Viktor Yanukovych, as the leaked Nuland-Pyatt call made clear. In April 2022, when negotiators in Istanbul came close to a peace agreement based on Ukrainian neutrality, the US and UK actually intervened to block the agreement. Today 75 percent of Ukrainians support negotiations with Russia to end the war.

In view of these causes of the war, I have recently set out a straightforward diplomatic framework for peace in Ukraine that would end the war. NATO would end its eastward expansion. Ukraine would adopt permanent neutrality on the model of Austria in 1955. An armistice line would be drawn, with both sides renouncing the use of force to change it. Ukraine would pursue membership in the European Union as a permanently neutral state. The Democrats should support such a diplomatic approach. It’s what can end the war, save Ukraine, and win the backing of both the Ukrainian and American people.

Most importantly, the Democrats should not mistake their victory for a mandate to pursue their own wars. The new Democratic majority should quickly reassert the constitutional authority of Congress over war and peace, champion a negotiated peace in Ukraine, end support for Israel’s wars, cut the military budget, and redirect the savings toward lowering the cost of living and repairing the public finances.

These positions are not only right but are good politics. For the Democrats to win the White House in 2028, they should become the party of peace. Better yet, both parties should become parties of peace and conduct the 2028 campaign on which party will best address America’s needs for decent jobs, affordability, healthcare, housing, a safe environment, and quality education.

Reprinted from Common Dreams.

Jeffrey D. Sachs is a University Professor and Director of the Center for Sustainable Development at Columbia University, where he directed The Earth Institute from 2002 until 2016. He is also President of the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network and a commissioner of the UN Broadband Commission for Development. He has been advisor to three United Nations Secretaries-General, and currently serves as an SDG Advocate under Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. Sachs is the author, most recently, of A New Foreign Policy: Beyond American Exceptionalism (2020). Other books include: Building the New American Economy: Smart, Fair, and Sustainable (2017), and The Age of Sustainable Development, (2015) with Ban Ki-moon.
